title: Review: Coordinates
description: Questions on the ideas in this chapter, from one star (a check of the definitions) to four stars (combining several ideas). They come in a random order each time.

questions.question: A point is $$5$$ to the right of the $$y$$-axis and $$2$$ below the $$x$$-axis. What are its coordinates?
questions.explanation: The $$x$$-coordinate comes first and says how far across, and below the $$x$$-axis the $$y$$-coordinate is negative (:ref{#coordinates}). So the point is $$(5, -2)$$.

questions.question: Which quadrant is the point $$(-6, 1)$$ in?
options: The first
The second
The third
The fourth
questions.explanation: Its $$x$$-coordinate is negative and its $$y$$-coordinate is positive, so it sits top left. The quadrants are numbered anticlockwise from the top right, which makes top left the second (:ref{#quadrants}). Numbering them clockwise would wrongly call it the fourth.

questions.question: Which quadrant is the point $$(0, -3)$$ in?
options: It is in no quadrant, since it lies on the $$y$$-axis
The third, since $$-3$$ is negative
The fourth, since $$0$$ counts as positive
Both the third and the fourth
questions.explanation: An $$x$$-coordinate of $$0$$ puts the point on the $$y$$-axis. The quadrants are made of the points on neither axis, so $$(0, -3)$$ is in none of them (:ref{#quadrants}).

questions.question: When do $$(a, b)$$ and $$(b, a)$$ name the same point?
options: Always, since they use the same two numbers
Never, since the order is different
Exactly when $$a = -b$$
Exactly when $$a = b$$
questions.explanation: By rule 1 of :ref{#coordinate-rules}, two pairs name the same point exactly when their first coordinates agree and their second coordinates agree. Here that says $$a = b$$. For example, $$(2, 3)$$ and $$(3, 2)$$ are different points.

questions.question: Which of these does the Coordinates guide take as given, rather than prove?
options: The distance formula
That $$(-3, 5)$$ is in the second quadrant
That each point has exactly one pair of coordinates, and every vertical line is perpendicular to every horizontal line
That the origin is $$(0, 0)$$
questions.explanation: Those facts are rules 1 and 3 of :ref{#coordinate-rules}, which are taken from the picture. The quadrant and the origin follow from the definitions, and the distance formula is proved from the rules in the next guide (:ref{#distance-formula}).

questions.question: The origin moves to the point that had coordinates $$(-1, 4)$$, and both axes keep pointing the same ways. What are the new coordinates of the point that was $$(3, 2)$$?
questions.explanation: Each point's new coordinates are its old ones minus the old coordinates of the new origin, so $$\big(3 - (-1), 2 - 4\big) = (4, -2)$$. Dropping the brackets gives $$3 - 1 = 2$$, and adding instead of subtracting gives $$(2, 6)$$. The points themselves don't move, only the axes they are read from (:ref{#coordinates}).

questions.question: Keep the origin, and turn both axes a quarter turn anticlockwise about it. What are the new coordinates of the point that was $$(2, 3)$$?
questions.explanation: The new $$x$$-axis points up, so the point's $$3$$ up becomes its new first coordinate. The new $$y$$-axis points left, so being $$2$$ to the right gives a second coordinate of $$-2$$. The answer $$(-3, 2)$$ is where the point would go if you turned the point instead of the axes (:ref{#coordinates}).

questions.question: Two surveyors put axes on the same field, one with the origin at the gate and one at an oak tree. Which of these must they agree on?
options: The distance between any two molehills
The coordinates of each molehill
Which quadrant each molehill is in
The $$x$$-coordinate of each molehill
questions.explanation: Coordinates depend on where the axes are put (:ref{#coordinates}), so the numbers and the quadrants can differ. Changing the axes doesn't move any point, so the distances stay the same.

questions.question: Why do these notes always put the positive $$y$$ direction a quarter turn anticlockwise from the positive $$x$$ direction?
options: The other choice would make the distance formula give different answers
Turning clockwise by a quarter turn is not possible in the plane
So that every figure drawn from coordinates comes out the same way round, not as a mirror image
Because computer screens use this convention
questions.explanation: With the other choice, a figure drawn from the same coordinates comes out flipped, a mirror image. Distances don't change under a flip, so the distance formula is unaffected. Screens use the opposite convention, with $$y$$ growing downwards (:ref{#coordinates}).

questions.question: What is the distance between $$(-1, 2)$$ and $$(5, 10)$$?
questions.explanation: The differences are $$5 - (-1) = 6$$ and $$10 - 2 = 8$$, so the distance is $$\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$$ (:ref{#distance-formula}). The answer $$100$$ forgets the square root, $$14$$ adds the legs as a taxi would, and $$\sqrt{80}$$ drops the brackets round $$-1$$.

questions.question: What is the distance between $$(-3, 1)$$ and $$(2, 1)$$?
questions.explanation: The points are level, so the distance is $$|2 - (-3)| = 5$$ (:ref{#line-distance}). Writing $$2 - 3$$ drops the brackets, a distance is never negative, and $$25$$ is the square of the distance.

questions.question: Why is $$\sqrt{(a - b)^2}$$ equal to $$|a - b|$$, and not always $$a - b$$?
options: A square root is never negative, so it gives the size of $$a - b$$ without its sign
They are always equal, since the root undoes the square
It is $$a - b$$ when $$a < b$$, and $$b - a$$ otherwise
Because $$(a - b)^2 = a^2 - b^2$$
questions.explanation: For $$a = 1$$ and $$b = 4$$, $$\sqrt{(-3)^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3$$, not $$-3$$. Part 1 of :ref{#line-distance} records this, and it is why the distance formula gives the same answer for level points as the number line.

questions.question: In the proof of :ref{#distance-formula}, why does the triangle $$PRQ$$, with $$R = (x_2, y_1)$$, have a right angle at $$R$$?
options: The angle is measured on the drawing
$$PR$$ lies on a horizontal line and $$RQ$$ on a vertical line, and every vertical line is perpendicular to every horizontal line
Because $$PQ$$ is the longest side
The distance formula says the sides fit the Pythagoras theorem
questions.explanation: $$P$$ and $$R$$ share the second coordinate $$y_1$$, and $$R$$ and $$Q$$ share the first coordinate $$x_2$$. Rule 3 of :ref{#coordinate-rules} makes those grid lines perpendicular. Using the distance formula here would be circular, since it is what the proof sets out to show.

questions.question: Why does the proof of the distance formula deal with level points, and points one above the other, separately?
options: The formula gives the wrong answer for them
Their distance is always zero
The Pythagoras theorem only holds for whole-number sides
Then $$P$$, $$R$$ and $$Q$$ don't make a triangle, so the Pythagoras theorem can't be used, and the distance along a grid line gives the answer instead
questions.explanation: If $$y_1 = y_2$$, the corner $$R$$ is $$Q$$ itself, and if $$x_1 = x_2$$, it is $$P$$, so there is no triangle. The formula still holds, and part 1 of :ref{#line-distance} shows it matches the distance along a grid line (:ref{#distance-formula}).

questions.question: Why can you subtract the coordinates in either order in the distance formula?
options: Subtraction gives the same answer either way round
You can't: always subtract the smaller coordinate from the larger
Swapping the order changes the sign of each difference, and squaring removes the sign
Coordinates are never negative
questions.explanation: $$x_1 - x_2 = -(x_2 - x_1)$$, and a number and its negative have the same square. So $$d(Q, P) = d(P, Q)$$, which agrees with rule 2 of :ref{#distance-and-angles/distance-rules}.

questions.question: How does the taxi distance $$|x_2 - x_1| + |y_2 - y_1|$$ compare with the straight-line distance?
options: The taxi distance is never shorter, and the two are equal exactly when the points are level or one above the other
The taxi distance is shorter whenever the points are far apart
They are always equal
The straight-line distance is longer whenever the route is diagonal
questions.explanation: The two legs and the straight path make a right triangle, and two sides of a triangle together are at least as long as the third (:ref{#distance-and-angles/distance-rules}). When one leg is $$0$$, there is no triangle and the two distances agree.

questions.question: A router at $$(1, -2)$$ reaches $$6$$ m. Is a laptop at $$(4, 2)$$ in range?
options: Out of range, since the squared distance $$25$$ is more than $$6$$
In range, since the squared distance $$25$$ is less than $$6^2 = 36$$
Out of range, since $$3 + 4 = 7$$ is more than $$6$$
You can't tell without working out a square root
questions.explanation: Distances and radii are never negative, so comparing their squares gives the same answer (:ref{#real-numbers/power-order}). The squared distance must be compared with $$r^2$$, not $$r$$, and $$7$$ is the taxi distance. The actual distance is $$\sqrt{25} = 5$$ (:ref{#distance-formula}).

questions.question: In the coordinate plane $$\mathbb{R}^2$$, what is the distance between two points?
options: The length a ruler measures on a drawing
A length taken as given, with no formula
A number defined to be $$\sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$
questions.explanation: In $$\mathbb{R}^2$$ points are pairs of numbers and the distance is defined to be the formula (:ref{#coordinate-plane}). That is what lets facts about distance be proved with algebra. The last option is the taxi distance.

questions.question: The Distance guide took the three rules for distance as given. Why does Geometry from numbers prove them?
options: The rules turned out to be false in the picture
The rules don't apply to the plane, only to lines
The distance formula was proved using these rules, so they had to come first
Distance is now defined by a formula, so each rule is a claim about the formula that algebra can check
questions.explanation: Once distance means the formula (:ref{#coordinate-plane}), a rule like the triangle inequality is a statement about square roots of numbers. It can be proved line by line, which is what :ref{#distance-zero}, :ref{#distance-symmetric} and :ref{#triangle-inequality-plane} do.

questions.question: Which fact shows that $$d(P, Q) = 0$$ forces $$P = Q$$?
options: A sum of two squares is $$0$$ exactly when both numbers being squared are $$0$$
A negative number has no square root
$$\sqrt{a + b} = \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$$
The triangle inequality
questions.explanation: $$d(P, Q) = 0$$ exactly when $$(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 = 0$$, and that happens exactly when both differences are $$0$$ (:ref{#distance-zero}). Then the coordinates match, so $$P = Q$$ by :ref{#coordinate-plane}.

questions.question: Is $$\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = a + b$$ for positive numbers $$a$$ and $$b$$?
options: Yes, the square root undoes the squares
Yes, as long as both numbers are whole
No: the left side is always the larger one
No: for $$a = 5$$ and $$b = 12$$, the left side is $$13$$ and the right side is $$17$$
questions.explanation: A square root of a sum doesn't split into a sum of square roots. That is why the proof of :ref{#triangle-inequality-plane} squares both sides instead of working with the roots directly. The left side is the smaller one, since a detour along the two legs is longer.

questions.question: In the proof of :ref{#triangle-inequality-plane}, what job does the lemma :ref{#product-bound} do?
options: It shows that distances are never negative
After both sides are squared, they differ only in their middle terms, and the lemma says the left one, $$2(as + bt)$$, is at most the right one
It shows that the steps of two trips add up to the steps of the direct route
It removes the square root from $$d(P, M)$$
questions.explanation: Squaring gives $$(a^2 + b^2) + 2(as + bt) + (s^2 + t^2)$$ on the left and the same with $$2\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\,\sqrt{s^2 + t^2}$$ in the middle on the right. :ref{#product-bound} compares exactly those middle terms.

questions.question: Why does the proof of :ref{#product-bound} treat the case $$as + bt < 0$$ on its own?
options: Because the inequality is false in that case
Because a negative number has no square root
Comparing squares only tells you the order of numbers that are not negative, and a negative number can have the larger square
Because $$a$$, $$b$$, $$s$$ and $$t$$ must all be positive
questions.explanation: For example, $$-5 < 3$$ but $$25 > 9$$. The step from squares back to numbers uses :ref{#real-numbers/power-order-converse}, which needs both numbers not negative. When $$as + bt < 0$$, the inequality holds anyway, since the right side is not negative.

questions.question: For which pair of steps $$(a, b)$$ and $$(s, t)$$ is $$as + bt$$ equal to $$\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\,\sqrt{s^2 + t^2}$$?
questions.explanation: The proof of :ref{#product-bound} shows the squares differ by $$(at - bs)^2$$, so they are equal exactly when $$at = bs$$. For $$(4, 10)$$, $$2 \cdot 10 = 5 \cdot 4$$, and $$as + bt = 58 = \sqrt{29}\,\sqrt{116}$$. The steps $$(-4, -10)$$ also have $$at = bs$$, but there $$as + bt = -58$$: equal squares, opposite signs.

questions.question: Why does the slide $$(x, y) \mapsto (x + h, y + k)$$ keep every distance in $$\mathbb{R}^2$$?
options: It is taken as given from the tracing paper
A slide doesn't change the coordinates of any point
Because $$h$$ and $$k$$ are positive
The $$h$$ and $$k$$ cancel when you subtract coordinates, so the differences in the distance formula don't change
questions.explanation: $$(x_2 + h) - (x_1 + h) = x_2 - x_1$$, and the same for $$k$$. The Isometries chapter took this from the tracing paper, but in $$\mathbb{R}^2$$ it is proved (:ref{#slide-distance}). The slide does change coordinates, and $$h$$ and $$k$$ can be any numbers.

questions.question: :ref{#origin-zoom} assumes $$r > 0$$. What does the same calculation give for the map $$(x, y) \mapsto (-2x, -2y)$$?
options: Every distance is multiplied by $$-2$$
Every distance stays the same
Every distance is multiplied by $$2$$, since $$\sqrt{(-2)^2} = 2$$
Nothing, because the proof breaks down completely
questions.explanation: Each difference of coordinates is multiplied by $$-2$$, so each square is multiplied by $$4$$, and $$\sqrt{4} = 2$$ comes out of the root. The proof of :ref{#origin-zoom} uses $$r > 0$$ to say $$\sqrt{r^2} = r$$. For a negative number the root of its square is its size, $$|r|$$, and a distance can't be negative.

questions.question: Which part of "$$(x, y) \mapsto (rx, ry)$$ is the zoom by $$r$$ about the origin" does Geometry from numbers leave for a later chapter?
options: That $$rP$$ is $$r$$ times as far from $$O$$ as $$P$$ is
That $$rP$$ lies on the ray from $$O$$ through $$P$$
That the zoom multiplies the distance between any two points by $$r$$
Nothing: every part is proved
questions.explanation: Taking $$Q = O$$ in :ref{#origin-zoom} proves the distance part. Lying on a ray is a fact about lines, and lines in coordinates come later.

questions.question: What is the centre of the circle $$(x + 3)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 16$$?
questions.explanation: The bracket $$(x + 3)$$ is $$\big(x - (-3)\big)$$, so $$a = -3$$, and $$(y - 2)$$ gives $$b = 2$$ (:ref{#circle-equation}). Each number in a bracket is the centre's coordinate with its sign changed.

questions.question: What is the radius of the circle $$(x - 1)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 10$$?
questions.explanation: The right side of the equation is $$r^2$$ (:ref{#circle-equation}). So $$r^2 = 10$$ and $$r = \sqrt{10}$$, about $$3.16$$.

questions.question: The proof of :ref{#circle-equation} goes from $$d(C, P)^2 = r^2$$ back to $$d(C, P) = r$$. Why is that step allowed?
options: Two numbers with equal squares are always equal
Because $$r^2$$ is positive
Both $$d(C, P)$$ and $$r$$ are not negative, and two numbers that are not negative with equal squares are equal
It isn't: the equation only shows one direction
questions.explanation: In general equal squares don't give equal numbers: $$(-3)^2 = 3^2$$. A distance and a radius are never negative, so :ref{#real-numbers/equal-squares} applies, and the equation works in both directions.

questions.question: Is the point $$(4, -1)$$ inside or outside the circle $$(x - 1)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 20$$?
options: Inside, since its distance from the centre is $$5$$, which is less than $$20$$
On the circle, since $$4 + 16 = 20$$
Inside, since $$25$$ is less than $$20^2$$
Outside, since $$9 + 16 = 25$$ is more than $$20$$
questions.explanation: By :ref{#disc-inequality}, compare the left side, $$3^2 + (-4)^2 = 25$$, with the right side $$r^2 = 20$$. The point is $$5$$ from the centre and the radius is $$\sqrt{20} \approx 4.47$$, so it is outside. The wrong options treat $$20$$ as the radius.

questions.question: Why does comparing $$(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2$$ with $$r^2$$ tell you whether a point is inside the circle?
options: Squaring always keeps the order of two numbers
Points inside a circle have smaller coordinates
It doesn't: you have to work out the square root
That sum is $$d(C, P)^2$$, and for numbers that are not negative, squaring keeps their order
questions.explanation: Squaring doesn't keep order in general: $$-4 < 3$$ but $$16 > 9$$. Distances and radii are never negative, so :ref{#real-numbers/power-order} and its converse apply (:ref{#disc-inequality}).

questions.question: Does every equation $$x^2 + y^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0$$ describe a circle?
options: No: after completing the square it may describe a circle, a single point, or no points at all
Yes, with radius $$\sqrt{F}$$
No: it is a circle exactly when $$F < 0$$
Yes, as long as the numbers in it are whole
questions.explanation: Completing the square gives $$\left(x + \frac{D}{2}\right)^2 + \left(y + \frac{E}{2}\right)^2 = c$$, and $$c$$ can be positive, zero or negative (:ref{#expanded-circle}). A negative $$F$$ does make $$c$$ positive, but $$x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 5 = 0$$ has $$F = 5$$ and is still a circle, with $$c = 4$$.

questions.question: What does $$x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 4y + 13 = 0$$ describe?
options: The circle with centre $$(-3, 2)$$ and radius $$\sqrt{13}$$
The single point $$(-3, 2)$$
No points at all
The circle with centre $$(6, -4)$$ and radius $$13$$
questions.explanation: Completing the square gives $$(x + 3)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 9 + 4 - 13 = 0$$. A sum of two squares is $$0$$ exactly when both are $$0$$, so only $$(-3, 2)$$ fits (:ref{#expanded-circle}). The constant $$13$$ is not $$r^2$$ until the squares are completed.

questions.question: What are the centre and radius of $$x^2 + y^2 - 8x + 2y - 8 = 0$$?
options: Centre $$(-8, 2)$$, radius $$\sqrt{8}$$
Centre $$(-4, 1)$$, radius $$5$$
Centre $$(4, -1)$$, radius $$5$$
Centre $$(4, -1)$$, radius $$25$$
questions.explanation: Completing the square, $$x^2 - 8x = (x - 4)^2 - 16$$ and $$y^2 + 2y = (y + 1)^2 - 1$$. So $$(x - 4)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 16 + 1 + 8 = 25$$, the circle with centre $$(4, -1)$$ and radius $$5$$ (:ref{#expanded-circle}).

questions.question: Where does the line $$y = 1$$ meet the circle with centre $$(1, -2)$$ and radius $$3$$?
options: At two points, since $$1 < 3$$
At the one point $$(1, 1)$$, since the line is exactly $$3$$ above the centre
Nowhere, since the centre is below the line
At the one point $$(1, -2)$$
questions.explanation: What matters is how far the line is from the centre, $$|k - b| = |1 - (-2)| = 3$$, not $$k$$ itself. That equals $$r$$, so the line touches the circle at $$(a, k) = (1, 1)$$ (:ref{#circle-horizontal-line}).

questions.question: For which numbers $$k$$ does the line $$y = k$$ cross the circle $$(x - 1)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 9$$ at two points?
questions.explanation: The centre is $$(1, -2)$$ and the radius is $$3$$, so the line crosses twice exactly when $$|k + 2| < 3$$ (:ref{#circle-horizontal-line}), that is, $$-5 < k < 1$$. The other options forget the centre, read its sign wrongly, or use $$r^2 = 9$$ as the radius.

questions.question: Which statement is the converse of the Pythagoras theorem?
options: If $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$, then the angle opposite $$c$$ is a right angle
If the angle opposite $$c$$ is a right angle, then $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$
$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$ for every triangle
If $$a + b = c$$, then the triangle has a right angle
questions.explanation: The Pythagoras theorem goes from a right angle to the equation (:ref{#distance-and-angles/pythagoras}). Its converse runs the other way, from the equation to the right angle (:ref{#pythagoras-converse}).

questions.question: Why does the converse of the Pythagoras theorem need its own proof?
options: It doesn't: it is the same statement written differently
Because the converse is false for some triangles
A statement read backwards is a different claim, and can be false when the original is true
Because it is only about whole numbers
questions.explanation: Every multiple of $$4$$ is even, but $$6$$ is even and not a multiple of $$4$$. So knowing a statement says nothing about its converse, and :ref{#pythagoras-converse} is proved separately.

questions.question: In the proof of :ref{#pythagoras-converse}, what does side, side, side (:ref{#isometries/sss}) do?
options: It shows that $$O$$, $$A$$ and $$B$$ have a right angle at $$O$$
It works out $$d(A, B) = c$$
It proves $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$
It gives an isometry from the given triangle to the right triangle on the axes, since their three sides match
questions.explanation: The right angle at $$O$$ comes from the axes, and $$d(A, B) = c$$ from the distance formula. Then the two triangles have equal sides, so side, side, side gives an isometry between them, and isometries keep angles (:ref{#isometries/isometry-angles}).

questions.question: A triangle has sides $$12$$, $$35$$ and $$37$$. Where is its right angle?
options: Between the sides $$12$$ and $$35$$, opposite the side $$37$$
Between the sides $$35$$ and $$37$$
It has none, since $$12 + 35 \ne 37$$
You can't tell without measuring an angle
questions.explanation: $$12^2 + 35^2 = 144 + 1225 = 1369 = 37^2$$, so by :ref{#pythagoras-converse} the angle opposite $$37$$ is a right angle. The test squares the sides, and three lengths are enough without measuring.

questions.question: Which of these is a rational point on the unit circle?
options: $$\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$$
$$\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$$
$$\left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right)$$
questions.explanation: A rational point has both coordinates rational (:ref{#rational-point}), and the unit circle needs $$x^2 + y^2 = 1$$. $$\frac{64 + 225}{289} = 1$$ for $$\left(\frac{8}{17}, \frac{15}{17}\right)$$. The points $$\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$$ and $$\left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right)$$ are rational but not on the circle, and $$\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$$ is on the circle but not rational.

questions.question: The line through $$(-1, 0)$$ with slope $$t = \sqrt{2}$$ meets the unit circle again at $$\left(-\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\right)$$. Is that a rational point?
options: Yes, since its first coordinate $$-\frac{1}{3}$$ is a fraction
No: its second coordinate is irrational, as part 3 of the theorem predicts for an irrational slope
Yes, since every line through a rational point meets the circle again at a rational point
The line doesn't meet the circle again
questions.explanation: Part 3 of :ref{#rational-points} says the second point is rational exactly when $$t$$ is rational. A rational point needs both coordinates rational (:ref{#rational-point}), and one rational coordinate is not enough.

questions.question: Why is the second point rational when the slope $$t$$ is rational?
options: The quadratic formula never involves square roots
Every point of the unit circle is a rational point
The quadratic for $$x$$ already has the solution $$x = -1$$, and the product of its two solutions is $$\frac{t^2 - 1}{1 + t^2}$$, so the other solution is a fraction built from $$t$$
Because the line passes through $$(0, 0)$$
questions.explanation: Knowing one solution and the product of both pins down the other: $$x_2 = \frac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}$$ (:ref{#rational-points}). Sums, products and quotients of fractions are fractions, so $$x_2$$ and $$y_2 = t(x_2 + 1)$$ are rational. Points like $$\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)$$ show that not every point is rational.

questions.question: Which slope $$t$$ gives the point $$\left(\frac{20}{29}, \frac{21}{29}\right)$$ as the second point of :ref{#rational-points}?
questions.explanation: The line goes through $$(-1, 0)$$, not the origin, so $$t = \frac{y}{x + 1} = \frac{21/29}{49/29} = \frac{21}{49} = \frac{3}{7}$$ (part 2 of :ref{#rational-points}). The slope $$\frac{21}{20}$$ is the line from the origin, and $$\frac{2}{5}$$ gives $$\left(\frac{21}{29}, \frac{20}{29}\right)$$, with the legs swapped.

questions.question: The triple $$12, 5, 13$$ has slope $$t = \frac{5}{12 + 13} = \frac{1}{5}$$. With $$m = 1$$ and $$n = 5$$, what does :ref{#triple-formula} say about it?
options: The formula gives $$12, 5, 13$$ itself, so $$k = 1$$
$$12, 5, 13$$ doesn't come from the formula at all
The formula gives $$24, 10, 26$$, so $$12, 5, 13$$ is that triple times $$k = \frac{1}{2}$$
The formula gives $$24, 10, 26$$, so $$k = 2$$
questions.explanation: $$n^2 - m^2 = 24$$, $$2mn = 10$$ and $$n^2 + m^2 = 26$$. Part 2 of :ref{#triple-formula} allows a rational multiplier $$k$$, and here $$k = \frac{13}{26} = \frac{1}{2}$$. Since $$2mn$$ is always even, a triple with an odd second leg can't come out of the formula with $$k = 1$$.

questions.question: A drone hovers at $$(12, 7, 30)$$, with $$z$$ measured upwards from the ground. Which point on the ground is directly below it?
questions.explanation: The points with the same first two coordinates make an upright line, and the ground is the layer $$z = 0$$ (:ref{#space-coordinate-rules}). So the spot below keeps $$x$$ and $$y$$ and has $$z = 0$$. The point $$(12, 7, -30)$$ is $$30$$ below the ground.

questions.question: How far is $$(2, 3, 6)$$ from the origin?
questions.explanation: By :ref{#space-distance}, the distance is $$\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7$$. Adding the coordinates gives $$11$$, leaving out the $$z$$ term gives $$\sqrt{13}$$, and $$49$$ forgets the square root.

questions.question: How does the proof of the distance formula in space use the Pythagoras theorem?
options: Once, in a right triangle with all three differences as its sides
It doesn't: the formula is taken as given
Three times, once for each axis
Twice: once for the diagonal across a flat layer, through the distance formula in the plane, and once in an upright right triangle
questions.explanation: The corner $$R = (x_2, y_2, z_1)$$ splits the trip into a step across the layer $$z = z_1$$, measured with :ref{#distance-formula}, and a climb straight up. Those two make a right triangle with $$PQ$$ as its hypotenuse (:ref{#space-distance}).

questions.question: In the proof of :ref{#space-distance}, which fact makes the triangle $$PRQ$$ have a right angle at $$R$$?
options: Each triple names exactly one point
The distance formula in the plane
An upright line is perpendicular to every line in a flat layer through the point where it crosses the layer
The triangle inequality
questions.explanation: $$RQ$$ is upright and $$PR$$ lies in the layer $$z = z_1$$, so rule 4 of :ref{#space-coordinate-rules} makes them perpendicular. That rule is the flagpole fact, taken as given.

questions.question: What does $$(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 + z^2 = 49$$ describe?
options: The sphere with centre $$(-2, 1, 0)$$ and radius $$7$$
The sphere with centre $$(2, -1, 0)$$ and radius $$7$$
The sphere with centre $$(2, -1, 0)$$ and radius $$49$$
Nothing, since there is no bracket for $$z$$
questions.explanation: $$z^2$$ is $$(z - 0)^2$$, so the centre's third coordinate is $$0$$, and each bracket's number has its sign changed (:ref{#sphere-equation}). The right side is $$r^2$$, so $$r = 7$$.

questions.question: The sphere with centre $$(0, 0, 5)$$ and radius $$13$$ meets the floor $$z = 0$$. What shape does it make there?
options: The circle with centre $$O$$ and radius $$12$$
The circle with centre $$O$$ and radius $$13$$
The circle with centre $$O$$ and radius $$8$$
Nothing, since the centre is above the floor
questions.explanation: Putting $$z = 0$$ into :ref{#sphere-equation} gives $$x^2 + y^2 + 25 = 169$$, so $$x^2 + y^2 = 144$$, the circle of radius $$12$$ (:ref{#circle-equation}). Radii combine through squares, so $$13 - 5 = 8$$ is wrong. The centre is $$5$$ above the floor and the radius is $$13$$, so the sphere reaches below it.

questions.question: A controller at the origin reaches $$50$$ m. Is a drone at $$(30, 40, 10)$$ in range?
options: In range, since the spot on the ground below it is exactly $$50$$ m away
In range, since height doesn't change the distance from the controller
Out of range, since the squared distance $$900 + 1600 + 100 = 2600$$ is more than $$50^2 = 2500$$
Out of range, since $$30 + 40 + 10 = 80$$ is more than $$50$$
questions.explanation: By :ref{#sphere-equation}, the drone is in range exactly when its squared distance is at most $$2500$$. The height adds $$10^2$$, which pushes it out of range. Adding the coordinates is not the distance, even though it happens to give the right verdict here.

questions.question: How does the distance between two points in space compare with the distance between the spots directly below them on the floor?
options: It is never shorter, and the two are equal exactly when the points are at the same height
It can be shorter, when one point is below the floor
They are always equal
It is always longer
questions.explanation: By :ref{#space-distance}, $$d(P, Q)^2$$ is the squared floor distance plus $$(z_2 - z_1)^2$$, which is never negative. The extra term is $$0$$ exactly when $$z_1 = z_2$$, whatever the signs of the heights.

questions.question: What changes when the triangle inequality is proved in space instead of the plane?
options: It needs a new idea, because space is not flat
Each step gets one more term: the lemma has three products, and the gap between the squares is a sum of three squares
It is taken as given in space
It fails in space
questions.explanation: The proof of :ref{#space-distance-rules} follows :ref{#triangle-inequality-plane} line by line. Its lemma, :ref{#product-bound-space}, has $$ap + bq + cs$$ in place of $$as + bt$$, and the gap is $$(aq - bp)^2 + (as - cp)^2 + (bs - cq)^2$$.
